C004.name: MR
C004.definition: MR is another term called mixed reality.

C005.name: headset
C005.definition: It is worn on the head, blocks our vision, and transports us to a virtual world which we can experience through the headset.

C006.name: Immersive technologies
C006.definition: These are technologies where the user experiences an environment through sensory organs in a way that makes them fail to distinguish it from reality.

C007.name: Immersive
C007.definition: It describes a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears to be real, causing the user to assume the environment is real.

C008.name: reality-virtuality continuum
C008.definition: It is essentially referring to a scale that spans from the real environment to the virtual environment.

C009.name: real environment
C009.definition: This is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing virtual.

C010.name: virtual environment
C010.definition: This is the other extreme of the scale where there is nothing real.

C011.name: augmented virtuality
C011.definition: Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where we are augmenting the virtual world with real world content.

C012.name: Metaverse
C012.definition: It is a concept that reimagines how humans interact with the digital world, moving beyond flat screens into an all-around 3D environment where users interact naturally.

C013.name: AR VR systems
C013.definition: These are the technologies that students will learn how to develop and deploy to master the field of virtual reality and augmented reality.

C014.name: Application areas
C014.definition: Application areas are the different areas pertaining to extended reality that the course will cover.

C015.name: Categories of systems
C015.definition: Categories of systems are different types of systems viewed from the application point of view that are present in the market.

C016.name: Use forecasts
C016.definition: Use forecasts are predictions about the likely scenario down the line in terms of application of extended reality technology.

C017.name: virtual tours
C017.definition: Virtual tours are experiences that give the user the experience of visiting a place without physically going there.

C018.name: virtual tourism
C018.definition: Virtual tourism is a popular method that allows users to explore faraway places while saving money and physical effort.

C019.name: heritage tourism
C019.definition: Heritage tourism allows users to visit a heritage place virtually, enabling them to explore every part of the space without physically going there.

C020.name: Non-immersive VR system
C020.definition: A virtual experience obtained through a computer where the user can control characters or activities within the software, but the environment is not directly interacting with the user.

C021.name: Augmentation of real-world content with digital content
C021.definition: This is the focus of AR, which involves adding digital content onto real-world content.

C022.name: Immersive experience
C022.definition: This is a term emphasized when discussing VR, but it is not mandatory in the case of AR.

C023.name: Reconstruction of lost structures
C023.definition: This is an interesting application area where lost structures can be added to the screen using AR.

C024.name: Virtual tape measure
C024.definition: This is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths without needing a physical tape.

C025.name: Customer experience
C025.definition: This refers to providing customers with the ability to test or visualize products in their environment before making a purchase decision.

C026.name: Telemedicine
C026.definition: This is an option that enables medical professionals to interact with patients using AR.

C027.name: VR system categories
C027.definition: These three categories (non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive) are based on the importance of the psychological aspect and user experience.

C028.name: Marker-based
C028.definition: These systems are easier to make and rely on simple algorithms, but they are difficult to maintain unless the environment is highly sanitized.

C029.name: Markerless
C029.definition: These techniques are used to overcome marker maintenance issues and primarily rely on computer vision, sometimes utilizing other sensors.

C030.name: Superimposition-based
C030.definition: This is a type of computer vision-based application used in AR.

C031.name: Projection-based techniques
C031.definition: These techniques, such as holographic projection, can be utilized in AR application development.

C032.name: Virtual
C032.definition: Being in essence or effect but not in fact.

C033.name: Reality
C033.definition: The state or quality of being real, or something that exists independently of ideas concerning it.

C034.name: Artificial environment
C034.definition: A computer-generated environment that may be populated with artificial objects.

C035.name: Sensory stimuli
C035.definition: Computer-generated inputs, such as sights and sounds, that allow the user to experience the artificial environment.

C036.name: Interaction
C036.definition: The dynamic change in the virtual environment that occurs based on the user's actions or inputs.

C037.name: VR system
C037.definition: A system is classified as a VR system only if it satisfies all three characteristics: virtual environment, immersive experience, and interaction.

C038.name: Characteristics of AR system
C038.definition: The defining features of an AR system, which include combining real with virtual, being interactive in real time, being registered in 3D, and being experienced through sensory organs.

C039.name: Overlay digital information
C039.definition: The process of placing digital information onto a representation of reality or an image of reality that is being viewed through a device.

C040.name: Registered in 3D
C040.definition: The requirement that digital content appears at the appropriate place when enhancing reality, allowing for seamless mixing with real-world objects.

C041.name: Augmented reality system
C041.definition: AR systems are the ones which augment or enhance our sense of reality.

C042.name: Formative years
C042.definition: This phase is roughly associated with the years between 1950 and 1990.

C043.name: Modern phase
C043.definition: This phase is defined as the period between 1991 and 2015.

C044.name: Growth phase
C044.definition: This is the current phase, which roughly started from 2016 onwards.

C045.name: Stereoscopic device
C045.definition: A stereoscopic device is a tool that allows the brain to process two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects.

C046.name: Immersion
C046.definition: Immersion is the state where 2D images are perceived as 3D objects or 3D space due to stereoscopic vision.

C047.name: Stereoscope
C047.definition: A stereoscope is a compact-sized device created to generate the illusion of depth when viewing images.

C048.name: Flight simulator
C048.definition: A flight simulator is a concept that uses multiple sensors to provide an immersive experience.

C049.name: HMDs or head-mounted displays
C049.definition: A new kind of computer display that people started working on in the 1950s.

C050.name: Sensorama
C050.definition: A device that tried to engage all our sensory organs, and is considered the first immersive virtual reality system.

C051.name: Haptic feedback
C051.definition: A sensation that allows the user to feel objects on the screen through touch.

C052.name: Virtual Visual Environment Display
C052.definition: The first commercially viable stereoscopic head-tracked HMD with a wide field of view.

C053.name: CAVE system
C053.definition: A system that renders images in a surrounding setting, giving an immersive experience.

C054.name: WTK package
C054.definition: A software package developed for higher level application development in VR.

C056.name: White 5
C056.definition: A 150-degree FOV field of view HMD.

C057.name: Oculus Rift
C057.definition: An inexpensive VR headset created in 2012.

C058.name: commercial VR headsets
C058.definition: These are well-known company releases starting around 2016 that made immersive experiences affordable to a large population, thereby spurring growth in the field.

C059.name: Experimental phase
C059.definition: This phase, which happened before the 1980s, was primarily related to early experimentation, defining concepts and showing different types of required technology.

C060.name: Basic research phase
C060.definition: This phase, occurring between the 1980s and mid-1990s, involved research into enabling technologies such as tracking, displays, and input devices.

C061.name: Tools or applications phase
C061.definition: During this phase, which ran from the mid-1990s to 2007, early applications and exploratory tasks related to interaction techniques and design theory were developed.

C062.name: Commercial application phase
C062.definition: This phase, starting from 2007 and continuing to date, is characterized by widespread AR availability and the emergence of newer applications in various domains.

C063.name: Tracking
C063.definition: Tracking technology is used to register content in 3D.

C064.name: Optical see-through head mounted display
C064.definition: This is a CRT-based display that allows the user to see through it while wearing it.

C065.name: Computer-generated imagery
C065.definition: This is imagery created by a computer that can be superimposed over the real world view or used as a substitute for the real world.

C066.name: Super cockpit program
C066.definition: This was a major program of the US Air Force that resulted in many relevant technologies for augmented reality.

C067.name: AR-type applications
C067.definition: These are precursors to the type of AR applications that are seen nowadays.

C068.name: Wearable computers
C068.definition: Wearable computers are setups where a headset is worn and the computer is carried in a backpack, utilizing various input devices.

C069.name: AR overlay on real-world markers
C069.definition: This involves using computer vision techniques to place augmented reality content onto real-world markers.

C070.name: Viewpoint tracking
C070.definition: Viewpoint tracking is the activity addressing the challenge of accurately tracking how the user's viewpoint is registered in 3D.

C071.name: AR Toolkit tracking library
C071.definition: This library provided real-time computer vision based tracking of a square marker.

C072.name: Mobile phone based AR application
C072.definition: This refers to the first demonstration of an augmented reality application utilizing a mobile phone.

C073.name: Commercial phase
C073.definition: This phase is characterized by AR experiences starting to become very popular, beginning with the launch of widely used consumer AR games.

C074.name: ARKit SDK
C074.definition: This is the SDK launched by Apple in 2017 for AR system development.

C075.name: ARCore
C075.definition: This is the SDK released by Google for Android OS or Android platforms.

C076.name: Commercial growth phase
C076.definition: This is the current phase where more applications and tools are expected to become available, with continuous improvements in hardware and algorithms.

C077.name: Issues and challenges
C077.definition: These are the problems and difficulties that exist within virtual and augmented reality systems.

C078.name: Synonyms
C078.definition: The terms augmented reality and mixed reality are used interchangeably and are considered synonyms.

C079.name: Virtual reality system
C079.definition: An artificial environment which is experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which one's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

C080.name: Objective of any VR system
C080.definition: To let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer.

C081.name: Technological issue
C081.definition: The challenge of how to generate suitable stimuli to experience the virtual or artificial environment.

C082.name: Psychological issue
C082.definition: The challenge of how the user perceives the generated stimuli, which relates to the role of the human factor and psychological characteristics.

C083.name: Immersion
C083.definition: Immersion is the objective degree to which a VR system and application projects stimuli onto the sensory receptors of users in a way that is extensive, matching, surrounding, vivid, interactive and plot informing.

C084.name: Extensive
C084.definition: Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user.

C085.name: Matching
C085.definition: Matching refers to the congruence between sensory modalities, such as appropriate visual presentation corresponding to head motion.

C086.name: Vivid
C086.definition: Vivid is the quality of energy stimulated within a particular modality, which relates to how much energy the computer is generating to stimulate that sensory organ.

C087.name: Interactivity
C087.definition: Interactivity refers to the capability of the user to make changes to the world, the response of virtual entities to user actions, and the user's ability to influence future events.

C088.name: Presence
C088.definition: Presence is a psychological state or subjective perception where the individual fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in their current experience.

C089.name: Qualities
C089.definition: These qualities refer to the activation of one or more sensory organs in a suitable way.

C090.name: Psychological side
C090.definition: The psychological side is the domain of presence, relating to the user's subjective perception of the experience.

C091.name: Overall goal of any virtual reality system
C091.definition: The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, making users feel they are in the virtual world and unable to distinguish it from the real world.

C092.name: Representational fidelity
C092.definition: It is the degree to which the VR experience conveys a place that is or could be on Earth.

C093.name: Combine real and virtual worlds
C093.definition: This requirement means that virtual content should be overlaid on the real world representation.

C094.name: Interactive in real time
C094.definition: This refers to supporting suitable forms of interaction so that the user can interact with the digital content overlaid on the real world representation.

C095.name: Pose
C095.definition: In this context, pose refers to two things: position and orientation.

C096.name: Registration phase
C096.definition: This phase determines the pose of a viewer with respect to the real world anchor.

C097.name: Tracking phase
C097.definition: This phase is necessary because the user is likely to move with an AR application, requiring continuous updates to the pose.

C098.name: Immersion
C098.definition: Immersion is tied to the technological aspect, the technological issues of VR.

C099.name: Cyber sickness
C099.definition: Cyber sickness is a concern that will be discussed in terms of its causes, measurement, and mitigation strategies.

C100.name: Visually Induced Motion Sickness
C100.definition: It is another name for cybersickness, a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality technology.

C101.name: Causes
C101.definition: This refers to the factors that lead to cybersickness.

C102.name: Evaluation
C102.definition: This refers to how we measure or assess cybersickness.

C103.name: Mitigation strategies
C103.definition: These are strategies that can be adopted to overcome the challenges associated with cybersickness.

C104.name: Stereoscopic vision
C104.definition: This is the experience of having vision through the HMDs, which is determined by the inter-pupillary distance (IPD).

C105.name: Latency
C105.definition: Latency is the time delay between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

C106.name: Latency jitter
C106.definition: Latency jitter is the variability in the time gap (latency) between a user's action in the physical world and its reflection in the virtual world.

C107.name: Visual motion stimulus
C107.definition: It is the movement experienced by the user in a virtual environment and is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness.

C108.name: Vection
C108.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion.

C109.name: Sensory mismatch
C109.definition: It occurs when users' virtual movements do not match their physical movements, resulting in discomfort and disorientation that leads to cyber sickness.

C110.name: Teleportation
C110.definition: Teleportation is an instantaneous transition between points in the virtual world.

C111.name: Visual complexity
C111.definition: It is a factor that is positively correlated to cyber sickness symptoms.

C112.name: Physiological or biometric input
C112.definition: These inputs are used to detect cybersickness and overcome the potential inaccuracies of subjective questionnaires.

C113.name: Behavioral input
C113.definition: This method detects cybersickness using behavioral cues such as blink rate, head and body movement, and postural sway.

C114.name: Content-based input
C114.definition: This refers to features related to the VR content that researchers study to evaluate cybersickness.

C115.name: Postural sway
C115.definition: This is a way to measure cybersickness by monitoring axial movements or changes in the user's center of pressure during VR exposure.

C116.name: Optical flow
C116.definition: This is the apparent motion perceived by VR users due to relative motion between the user and the environment.

C117.name: Manual evaluation
C117.definition: Manual evaluation is a measurement technique based on human intervention, typically involving the distribution and analysis of questionnaires.

C118.name: Machine learning-based evaluation
C118.definition: This evaluation method uses automated algorithms on the input data to measure cyber sickness.

C119.name: Transparent models
C119.definition: These models provide clear insight into the decision-making process and their inner workings can be easily understood.

C120.name: cybersickness
C120.definition: Cybersickness is the primary topic of discussion in this lecture segment.

C121.name: evaluation techniques
C121.definition: Evaluation techniques are methods used to measure and evaluate cybersickness.

C122.name: input
C122.definition: Input is one of the three broad aspects of evaluation, referring to the data provided.

C123.name: process
C123.definition: Process is one of the three broad aspects of evaluation, referring to the evaluation procedure itself.

C124.name: output
C124.definition: Output is one of the three broad aspects of evaluation, referring to the kind of results expected from the evaluation process.

C125.name: Interpretable models
C125.definition: These models offer more flexibility in customization and provide precise details about the relationships between the input and output.

C126.name: Hybrid models
C126.definition: They are combinations of different ML models designed to provide both high accuracy and transparency in their decision-making process.

C127.name: Detection
C127.definition: Detection refers to the process of identifying cyber sickness after it has already occurred.

C128.name: Prediction
C128.definition: Prediction involves anticipating cyber sickness before it happens.

C129.name: Classification
C129.definition: Classification indicates the likelihood or severity of cyber sickness, such as low, moderate, or acute.

C130.name: Sickness score
C130.definition: A sickness score is a numerical value that quantifies the severity of the cyber sickness experience.

C131.name: Severity of CS
C131.definition: The severity of cyber sickness is assessed based on the scores or ratings provided.

C132.name: Mitigation
C132.definition: Mitigation is the third aspect of cyber sickness, focusing on measures taken to reduce or eliminate its impact when complete prevention is not possible.

C133.name: Trade-off
C133.definition: A trade-off is the decision of whether to completely avoid cyber sickness by reducing presence or to balance the compromise between the two.

C134.name: Developer's perspective
C134.definition: The developer's perspective focuses on what developers can do or how they can address the problem.

C135.name: User's perspective
C135.definition: The user's perspective focuses on what users can do, regardless of the quality of the solution.

C136.name: FOV adjustment
C136.definition: Adjusting the field of view means changing the amount of virtual environment visible at any moment, which can mitigate the onset or severity of cyber sickness.

C137.name: Symmetric mask
C137.definition: This is a technique where the periphery is occluded in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity.

C138.name: Blurring
C138.definition: Blurring means obscuring or reducing the clarity.

C139.name: Depth of field blur
C139.definition: Depth of field blur makes use of well-known depth cues in human vision.

C140.name: Peripheral blur
C140.definition: Peripheral blur is one of the two types of blur effects.

C141.name: Rest frames
C141.definition: Rest frames are fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements.

C142.name: Independent visual backgrounds
C142.definition: Independent visual backgrounds are rest frames attached to the head reference frame.

C143.name: Simultaneous presentation of sound and vibration
C143.definition: This involves providing sound and vibration at the same time.

C144.name: Modified motion platforms
C144.definition: These platforms can be modified to provide short bursts of rotational acceleration that match the visual forward acceleration.

C145.name: Viewpoint snapping
C145.definition: This technique involves rendering moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation.

C146.name: Habituation
C146.definition: The intensity of cyber sickness gradually decreases after repeated experience in the virtual environment.

C147.name: Slow diaphragmatic breathing
C147.definition: Controlling breathing patterns to a large extent, reducing the possibility of cyber sickness.

C148.name: External causes
C148.definition: These causes can be related to hardware or content.

C149.name: Evaluation strategies
C149.definition: These strategies involve inputs (manual or automated through machine learning), a process, and outputs (classes, CS scores, or numerical values).

C150.name: organism
C150.definition: In the context of a VR system, the organism typically refers to the human user.

C151.name: stimulation
C151.definition: Stimulation is the process where the hardware produces stimuli that override the senses of the user.

C152.name: Surrounding physical world
C152.definition: The surrounding physical world must be taken into account as part of the VR system because the user may respond to stimuli from it.

C153.name: Head tracking
C153.definition: Head tracking is the most important thing to track when discussing tracking in VR.

C154.name: VR hardware
C154.definition: VR hardware should not be restricted to only the computer, HMD, or controller used by the user.

C155.name: Trackers
C155.definition: Trackers or sensors are hardware components that can track objects in the surroundings rather than the user directly.

C156.name: Display
C156.definition: It can mean any device that produces output that stimulates users' sensory organs.

C157.name: world grounded devices
C157.definition: These are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move.

C158.name: non-tracked handheld controllers
C158.definition: These are devices held in hand, but the system does not track their exact position in 3D space.

C159.name: tracked handheld controllers
C159.definition: These are devices that possess 6 degrees of freedom tracking, allowing their movements to be tracked by the system.

C160.name: bend sensing gloves
C160.definition: These gloves detect hand postures and gestures because sensors are placed at all bend positions or joints.

C161.name: pinch gloves
C161.definition: In pinch gloves, sensors are placed only at the fingertip positions, typically to detect pinching gestures.

C162.name: bare hand inputs
C162.definition: This method tracks the bare hand using computer vision techniques, allowing users to provide gestures without wearing external devices.

C163.name: non-hand-based input devices
C163.definition: These types of devices capture input from other parts of the body other than the hand.

C164.name: head tracking based input devices
C164.definition: These devices typically use our head motion for input.

C165.name: eye trackers
C165.definition: These devices are typically used to track eye movements, allowing the system to infer what to do and take necessary action.

C166.name: Midas touch problem
C166.definition: This is an issue where it is difficult to understand whether a user's action is intentional or by nature.

C167.name: Full-body tracking
C167.definition: This method tracks more than just the head and hands, which adds to the illusion of self-embodiment as well as social presence.

C168.name: Motion capture suit
C168.definition: A suit containing a network of straps with IMU sensors worn at different body parts that capture and transmit raw movement data converted to full body position and movement.

C169.name: Camera-based tracking
C169.definition: This approach uses multiple surrounding cameras to detect the movement of fiducial markers worn by an actor to infer the overall body movement of the character.

C170.name: Voice or speech or sound tracking
C170.definition: This input type captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound as input for interaction in the virtual world.

C171.name: Computer
C171.definition: A device that processes data coming from input sensors and then activates or actuates the output devices.

C172.name: GPU
C172.definition: A graphics processing unit typically used to speed up the rendering process due to its inherent parallel processing abilities.

C173.name: Multicore processor
C173.definition: A processor that can greatly increase computational capacity and support tasks better than non-multicore or unicore processors.

C174.name: Head-mounted displays
C174.definition: HMDs are wearable and mobile displays meant to stimulate the visual sense.

C175.name: World-fixed displays
C175.definition: World-fixed displays are stationary displays that are not wearable and render graphics onto surfaces that do not move with the head.

C176.name: Monoscopic viewing
C176.definition: Monoscopic viewing is the process of viewing images when the display is using only one screen.

C177.name: Stereoscopic viewing
C177.definition: Stereoscopic viewing is the process of viewing images when the display is using two screens.

C178.name: Haptics
C178.definition: Haptics are outputs that explore our touch perception.

C179.name: Passive device
C179.definition: Passive devices are static physical objects.

C180.name: Active device
C180.definition: Active devices are physical feedback controlled by the computer.

C181.name: Tactile
C181.definition: Tactile refers to touch sensations obtained through the skin.

C182.name: Self-grounded device
C182.definition: Self-grounded devices are worn or held by and move with the user.

C183.name: Passive motion platform
C183.definition: A motion platform that is controlled by the user, without direct computer control.

C184.name: Omnidirectional treadmills
C184.definition: A type of treadmill that is quite common in virtual reality systems.

C185.name: Proprioceptive forces
C185.definition: One of the types of output devices used in VR systems.

C186.name: Headsets and glasses
C186.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices used to provide AR experience.

C187.name: Handheld devices
C187.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices, such as smartphones and tablets.

C188.name: Projection-based systems
C188.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices that includes projection keyboards, interactive projectors, AR sandboxes, industrial AR systems, and medical systems.

C189.name: Spatial AR
C189.definition: This is a category of augmented reality devices that includes interactive projectors and AR sandboxes.

C190.name: Head-up displays
C190.definition: These are devices typically found in cars that are being explored for AR systems.

C191.name: AR contact lenses
C191.definition: This is the latest technology being explored for AR systems, with ongoing research by various companies.

C192.name: Projection keyboard
C192.definition: This is a system that projects a virtual keyboard onto any surface, allowing users to type as if they were using a physical keyboard.

C193.name: Interactive projector
C193.definition: It projects images onto any surface, thereby turning that surface into an interactive display and creating an AR experience.

C194.name: AR headsets
C194.definition: AR headsets are generally larger and more immersive, combining both real-world content and augmented digital content.

C195.name: glasses
C195.definition: These are special types of glasses where real digital content can be projected on top of our regular real-world view.

C196.name: high-definition holograms
C196.definition: High-definition holograms or digital content are integrated with the real-world view.

C197.name: interaction
C197.definition: Interaction in AR, such as with HoloLens, takes place through eye movements, voice commands, and hand motions.

C198.name: smart glasses
C198.definition: Smart glasses are typically lighter than AR HMDs, resemble standard eyeglasses, and provide simpler heads-up display type AR digital content overlays.

C199.name: Augmentation
C199.definition: The process where digital content is overlaid onto the live streaming of the real world environment.

C200.name: Marker-based AR
C200.definition: A type of AR where the system recognizes specific markers placed in the real world to augment content.

C201.name: Spatial augmented reality devices
C201.definition: The third category of AR devices mentioned in the lecture.

C202.name: Computer vision techniques
C202.definition: These are advanced techniques typically used in spatial AR systems to achieve seamless mixing.

C203.name: Room-scale AR or tabletop AR
C203.definition: These are alternative names for the devices being discussed in this segment.

C204.name: Seamless mixing
C204.definition: This is the ability to blend virtual and physical elements without disruption, which requires understanding the physical environment's geometry and lighting conditions.

C205.name: Depth sensors
C205.definition: These are advanced sensors typically used in spatial AR systems to achieve seamless mixing.

C206.name: Multi-user engagement with AR systems
C206.definition: This is the characteristic where multiple users can work together on the augmented digital content.

C207.name: Spatial AR systems
C207.definition: Spatial AR systems are characterized by distinct features and functionalities.

C208.name: HUDs
C208.definition: HUDs are commonly seen in cars and are also frequently used in aircraft.

C209.name: Sensing
C209.definition: Sensing is another term often used to describe the requirement of tracking in XR systems.

C210.name: Tracking hardware
C210.definition: Tracking hardware refers to the entire hardware components typically used in XR applications for tracking.

C211.name: User's pose, position, and orientation
C211.definition: These are the specific elements that AR requires keeping track of.

C212.name: Tracking of the user's sense organs
C212.definition: This category involves tracking the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, whose degrees of freedom are controlled by the body.

C213.name: Tracking the user's other body parts
C213.definition: This category tracks body parts other than sense organs, which is required when the user wants to see a representation of the body in the virtual world.

C214.name: Tracking the rest of the environment
C214.definition: This category involves tracking physical objects in the real world surrounding the user, which is particularly important in Augmented Reality.

C215.name: Outside-in tracking
C215.definition: This type of tracking occurs when the trackers or sensors are placed within the real world external to the user, not attached to the user.

C216.name: Calibration
C216.definition: Calibration is the process of transforming sensor output to behave as closely to the real value as possible.

C217.name: Registration
C217.definition: Registration is the step where the initial sensor position and orientation are estimated or determined.

C218.name: Integration
C218.definition: Integration is the step where sensory measurements are aggregated or combined at discrete points of time.

C219.name: Drift correction
C219.definition: Drift correction means compensating for differences between the estimated tracking and the actual position and orientation.

C220.name: Inside-out tracking
C220.definition: In inside-out tracking, the tracker carries the sensors that are part of the devices that the user is wearing or using.

C221.name: Inside-out
C221.definition: Inside-out trackers have all the sensors placed on the device that the user is using.

C222.name: Outside-in
C222.definition: Outside-in trackers have sensors placed in the surrounding environment rather than on the device that the user is using.

C223.name: IMU sensor
C223.definition: An IMU sensor is a composite hardware containing three types of sensors: gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer.

C224.name: gyroscope
C224.definition: A gyroscope is a sensor that captures the angular velocity.

C225.name: accelerometer
C225.definition: An accelerometer is a sensor that captures the linear acceleration along the three axes (x, y, and z).

C226.name: magnetometer
C226.definition: A magnetometer is a sensor that captures magnetic field strength along the three axes.

C227.name: Measurement error
C227.definition: Measurement error is the difference between the measured angular velocity ($\omega_g$) and the actual angular velocity ($\omega_a$).

C228.name: Linear relationship
C228.definition: A linear relationship is a proposed mathematical model between the measured angular velocity ($\omega_g$) and the actual angular velocity ($\omega_a$) in the form $\omega_g = a + b \cdot \omega_a$.

C229.name: Linear least squares
C229.definition: Linear least squares is a classical regression problem used to optimize the square term of the difference between the sensor readings during calibration.

C230.name: Initial orientation
C230.definition: The initial orientation is the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is turned on, which sets the initial alignment.

C231.name: Alignment
C231.definition: Alignment is the setting of the initial alignment between the real and virtual worlds, represented symbolically by theta at time t=0.

C232.name: Calibrated angular velocity sample
C232.definition: This is the angular velocity sample obtained from the gyroscopic sensor at a specific instant.

C233.name: gain parameter
C233.definition: The gain parameter (alpha) is a normalized value between 0 to 1 used to combine individually computed orientations.

C234.name: theta dk
C234.definition: Theta dk is the drift-corrected orientation at time instant t.

C235.name: theta gk
C235.definition: Theta gk is the orientation obtained by integrating gyroscope values at the kth instant.

C236.name: theta ck
C236.definition: Theta ck is the orientation obtained with camera at kth instant.

C237.name: Electromechanical trackers
C237.definition: These trackers consist of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints with sensors.

C238.name: World-fixed
C238.definition: This type of electromechanical tracker is a setup that is not worn on the body of the user.

C239.name: Wearable trackers
C239.definition: These are electromechanical trackers that can be worn on the body of the user.

C240.name: Electromagnetic trackers
C240.definition: It is a kind of non-contact position measurement device that uses a magnetic field from a stationary transmitter to determine the real-time position of a moving receiver element.

C241.name: Acoustic tracking
C241.definition: This tracking method uses ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters to determine the real-time position.

C242.name: Ultrasonic tracking
C242.definition: This is a method that uses ultrasonic signals produced by stationary transmitters to determine real time position.

C243.name: Non-contact position measurement device
C243.definition: This device tracks position without physical contact, such as electromagnetic trackers.

C244.name: vision-based tracker
C244.definition: This is a category of tracker that is considered the most important in the present context.

C245.name: optical sensors
C245.definition: These sensors are deployed to detect or track the pose.

C246.name: infrared tracking
C246.definition: This is a vision-based tracking technique that uses targets that emit or reflect light.

C247.name: outside looking in
C247.definition: In this method, targets are attached to objects being tracked, but the cameras are external to the object and placed in the environment.

C248.name: Fiducials
C248.definition: Fiducials are artificial landmarks added to the environment to aid in registration and tracking.

C249.name: Fiducial tracking
C249.definition: Fiducial tracking involves adding artificial landmarks in the environment so that one can track whatever is desired.

C250.name: Descriptors
C250.definition: Descriptors are unique calculations made for each feature to allow for identification and differentiation from other features.

C251.name: SLAM
C251.definition: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it.

C252.name: 3D structure tracking
C252.definition: This technique involves creating 3D models of the structures present in the environment and using them for augmentation of the real-world view.

C253.name: 3D models
C253.definition: These are high-quality representations created from data obtained by sensors of real objects and environments.

C254.name: Augmentation of the real-world view
C254.definition: This is the process of using 3D models of environmental structures to enhance the real-world view.

C255.name: inertial trackers
C255.definition: These are self-contained sensors that measure rate of change in object orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration.

C256.name: primary sensors
C256.definition: These are the basic sensors used in inertial tracking, specifically gyroscopes, accelerometer, and magnetometer.

C257.name: acoustic sensing
C257.definition: This is one type of sensing that does not directly fit into the previously listed categories of trackers.

C258.name: GPS
C258.definition: GPS is a positional tracking device that allows us to track positions.

C259.name: RTK
C259.definition: RTK, or real time kinematic technology, uses GPS signal carrier waves for measurement to provide further accuracy compared to the basic GPS system.

C260.name: Motion capture
C260.definition: The technique of digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans.

C261.name: Eye-tracking systems
C261.definition: Trackers that typically track the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

C262.name: Non-real-time tracking
C262.definition: Tracking that does not need to be real-time.

C263.name: Hybrid trackers
C263.definition: Any other tracker that can be roughly called hybrid.

C264.name: VR software
C264.definition: The role of VR software is to drive the hardware to generate an experience utilizing our senses.

C265.name: Modeling of the environment
C265.definition: Modeling of the environment is the activity of creating the virtual environment.

C266.name: Rendering
C266.definition: Rendering is the creation of the stereoscopic view, which refers broadly to output for various senses.

C267.name: Perceptual design
C267.definition: Perceptual design ensures that stimuli generated by the hardware can suitably stimulate our sense organs.

C268.name: VR engine
C268.definition: The VR engine is one of the two components of the software that handles the data flow between the user and the system.

C269.name: High-level descriptions
C269.definition: Descriptions provided by the developer that the supporting software automatically converts into low-level details.

C270.name: Middleware
C270.definition: A layer that can exist between the developer and the hardware.

C271.name: Software development kit
C271.definition: A kit utilized for particular headsets that handles low-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output.

C272.name: Platform
C272.definition: A combination of hardware and OS upon which SDKs are dependent.

C273.name: Game engine
C273.definition: Middleware specifically created or adapted for VR experience generation.

C274.name: Virtual World Generator
C274.definition: The VWG is an abstraction of the whole software system whose key role is to maintain internal reality and convert input information to output so that it appears real to the user.

C275.name: Internal reality
C275.definition: Internal reality is the state that the VWG must maintain so that the virtual world appears real to the user.

C276.name: Abstraction
C276.definition: The whole software system can be thought of as an abstraction, specifically a virtual world generation abstraction.

C277.name: Input/output match
C277.definition: The role of the VR VWG is to maintain the match between the input information and the resulting output.

C278.name: Input events
C278.definition: Input events are data arriving from low-level systems that must be arranged in a queue ready to be processed systematically.

C279.name: Queue
C279.definition: A queue is a mechanism used to arrange multiple simultaneous input events so that they can be processed systematically.

C280.name: Haptic renderer
C280.definition: A device that generates haptic display to be sensed with our skin.

C281.name: Triangular mesh
C281.definition: A structure of numerous triangles in a 3D space that must be created to form a synthetic scene.

C282.name: Computer graphics
C282.definition: The field that addresses computer-generated images from synthetic models.

C283.name: Texture mapping
C283.definition: The process of taking camera images of a real object and mapping them onto a synthetic object in the virtual world.

C284.name: matched motion
C284.definition: It is the correspondence maintained between user motions in the real and virtual world.

C285.name: matched zone
C285.definition: It is a region where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align, and the user's physical movement is restricted.

C286.name: locomotion
C286.definition: It is moving oneself in the virtual world while the motion is not matched in the real world.

C287.name: User locomotion
C287.definition: User locomotion is the method of moving oneself within the virtual world, often by operating input devices like controllers or keyboards.

C288.name: Avatar
C288.definition: The avatar is the user's representation in the virtual world that can perform activities like walking, running, or swimming without the user moving physically.

C289.name: Vehicle metaphor
C289.definition: The vehicle metaphor is a way to allow the user to move in the virtual world by operating the controls of a virtual vehicle while remaining seated.

C290.name: Key components
C290.definition: Key components are the essential elements that VR software should support, primarily from the developer's point of view.

C291.name: Desirable components of the virtual world generator
C291.definition: The necessary parts that should be included within the virtual world generator concept.

C292.name: Synthetic virtual world generation
C292.definition: The generation of a virtual world that requires support for computer graphics operations.

C293.name: Matched motion and locomotion
C293.definition: A required support concept for movement within the virtual world.

C294.name: Physics support
C294.definition: Physics support is the required functionality to make the virtual world appear to behave like the real world, governed by basic laws of mechanics.

C295.name: Collision
C295.definition: Collision is the event of one object interacting with other objects.

C296.name: Collision detection algorithm
C296.definition: The collision detection algorithm determines whether two or more bodies are intersecting in the virtual world and how they should behave if they are.

C297.name: Collision response
C297.definition: Collision response is the appropriate action that must occur after a collision takes place.

C298.name: Shared virtual world
C298.definition: A virtual world that is maintained by a system or a server.

C299.name: Matched zone
C299.definition: A distinct area assigned to each user within the virtual world.

C300.name: Collaborative VR experience
C300.definition: A collaborative experience that is created over a network.

C301.name: Physics
C301.definition: The algorithms and support required to handle problems such as avatar movement, collision detection, and the response to collisions.

C302.name: Game engine
C302.definition: A popular engine adapted to work for virtual reality that comes with built-in supports for features like collisions and physics.

C303.name: Native application
C303.definition: A native application requires the use of SDKs that are tailored specifically to the platform and the hardware.

C304.name: HMD
C304.definition: HMDs, or head-mounted displays, are the most popular device types used for VR experiences.

C305.name: Cloud hosting and rendering
C305.definition: These tools only provide support for hosting and rendering over a network.

C306.name: Libraries
C306.definition: Libraries are tools used for development support, specifically for deployment over the web.

C307.name: SDKs
C307.definition: SDKs are one of two developer choices for building VR applications, allowing development from scratch.

C308.name: Deployment tools
C308.definition: These are tools available for deploying applications, either on native systems or over the web.

C309.name: low-level software libraries
C309.definition: These libraries require considerable skill from the developer, both in understanding the library functions and in coding to call them.

C310.name: simple authoring tools
C310.definition: These tools assume that the developer does not have any programming skill and are typically intended for novice developers or users.

C311.name: Framework for AR system development
C311.definition: This is a combination of multiple libraries created to overcome the limitations of standard toolkits and enable realistic AR system development.

C312.name: Scene graphs
C312.definition: Scene graphs represent computer graphic scenes as a node-based graph, allowing the entire scene to be represented as a tree with nodes and links.

C313.name: 3D registration
C313.definition: 3D registration is the process of creating and rendering a 3D object at a specific position based on tracking data.

C314.name: Low-level OpenGL-based rendering support
C314.definition: This support provides very primitive rendering capabilities without built-in support for interaction techniques or complex realistic graphics.

C315.name: ARToolKit
C315.definition: This library is primarily meant to provide tracking support for developing AR applications.

C316.name: Rapid prototyping
C316.definition: The process of rapidly visualizing or creating prototypes of an idea before undertaking major coding development, which helps determine if the idea is viable.

C317.name: FLAR Toolkit
C317.definition: A version of an AR toolkit ported over to Flash that allows users to have an AR experience from within their web browser.

C318.name: Flash AR Manager
C318.definition: A framework that combines a variety of different AR tracking and graphics libraries together, primarily for prototyping purposes.

C319.name: Open Frameworks
C319.definition: It is an open-source C++ middleware library that is a combination of multiple libraries meant for desktop and mobile platforms.

C320.name: Client device
C320.definition: A mobile device that is primarily treated as a client device, meaning actual computation may take place on a backend server.

C321.name: Rendering device
C321.definition: A mobile device that is primarily treated as a rendering device, handling visual output.

C322.name: Backend server
C322.definition: A server where actual computation may take place, rather than on the mobile device.

C323.name: Plugins to existing tools
C323.definition: Plugins are additions that provide AR-specific functionalities to software tools that the user is already familiar with.

C324.name: AR visualization
C324.definition: This refers to the process of creating interactive 3D applications using tools and plugins.

C325.name: Plugin-based approach
C325.definition: This approach provides an easy and quick method for developing AR applications, but it can limit flexibility in design and depend on proprietary software.

C326.name: Authoring tool
C326.definition: An authoring tool is a graphics tool used to create interactive 3D applications and provides underlying support for development.

C327.name: Proprietary player software
C327.definition: This is software that content produced with an authoring tool must depend on in most cases to be played.

C328.name: Low-level software development tools
C328.definition: These tools allow developers to build their own system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool to resolve issues with high-level tools.

C329.name: Plugins
C329.definition: Plugins require a basic authoring tool to function, providing AR support through that underlying tool.

C330.name: Graphical user interface
C330.definition: These are typically drag-and-drop type interfaces that allow developers to create an experience without requiring coding.

C331.name: Web-based authoring tool
C331.definition: This is an authoring tool that operates via the web, such as Wikitude Studio.

C332.name: AR software
C332.definition: This is the subject of the discussion, covering the basic idea of how it functions.

C333.name: Categories
C333.definition: These are classifications of tools and packages based on the programming skill required to use them.

C334.name: Low-level libraries and frameworks
C334.definition: These are tools that require the highest programming skill to deal with.

C335.name: Rapid prototyping tools
C335.definition: These are tools that fall into a category between the extremes of high and low programming skill requirements.

C336.name: Human factors
C336.definition: This is a topic that affects the experience when building and deploying Extended reality systems.

C337.name: Technology disappearing
C337.definition: The vision of making the technology disappear from the user's point of view.

C338.name: IoT or ubiquitous computing
C338.definition: A state where each user can have access to multiple connected computers that communicate with each other so the user does not have to separately operate them.

C339.name: Interactive computing systems
C339.definition: Systems where interaction takes place between the computer or the system and the user.

C340.name: Lay person
C340.definition: A user who is not necessarily an expert in the technology but simply wants to use the system.

C341.name: Interactions
C341.definition: Interactions are designed to fulfill the needs of the users by taking them to the desired system states.

C342.name: Interactive system
C342.definition: A system designed for laypersons should not force the user to learn the underlying technology or understand relevant technical terms.

C343.name: Layouts
C343.definition: Layouts are the way the elements are organized on the screen or on the interface that meet the user's expectations.

C344.name: System state
C344.definition: The system state is what exactly is happening from the point of view of the user, not from the point of view of technical details.

C345.name: Goal state
C345.definition: The goal state is the state reached after transitioning from one state to another until the user reaches some goal.

C346.name: Interface elements
C346.definition: Interface elements are the elements with which the user interacts that are acceptable to the users.

C347.name: user characteristics
C347.definition: This is the knowledge of the user that must be utilized to build the system.

C348.name: human-computer interaction
C348.definition: It is a discipline concerned with the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use and with the study of major phenomena surrounding them.

C349.name: core concern
C349.definition: The core concern is incorporating humans into the design.

C350.name: human factors
C350.definition: This is an important issue that requires understanding users to design systems effectively.

C351.name: Novice
C351.definition: Novice users are those who are using the system for the first time.

C352.name: Intermittent
C352.definition: Intermittent users are those who use the system occasionally.

C353.name: Expert
C353.definition: Expert users are those who are experts in using the system, having used it for quite some time and understood all aspects of the system.

C354.name: Usability
C354.definition: It is the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals, with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C355.name: User interface or user experience designer
C355.definition: Such a designer is primarily concerned about the design of the interface elements and layouts, which is mostly a creative design aspect, informed by user characteristics.

C356.name: Industrial product designer
C356.definition: This designer refers to the form of the product that is shape, size and look.

C357.name: Electronic engineer
C357.definition: This designer might look at it as adding more features at the hardware level such as more sensors, smaller chips to reduce size and more power efficient battery, primarily from the hardware point of view.

C358.name: Development lifecycle
C358.definition: This is a process that takes care of the user characteristics to better match the user's needs and expectations.

C359.name: Effectiveness
C359.definition: Effectiveness refers to whether the user is able to do whatever they want to do.

C360.name: Efficiency
C360.definition: Efficiency refers to how fast the user can do what they want to do.

C361.name: Satisfaction
C361.definition: Satisfaction refers to how satisfied the user is when they are using the system.

C362.name: User-centered design
C362.definition: User-centered design indicates the involvement of users, either in an active or passive manner, in the design lifecycle itself.

C363.name: Extended reality systems
C363.definition: The core concern of extended reality software is to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment.

C364.name: Interaction design and modeling
C364.definition: This approach assists the user to provide input data seamlessly, effectively, and easily from the user's point of view.

C365.name: Perceptual design and modeling
C365.definition: This is crucial for determining how well the output is generated, ensuring that input and output match.

C366.name: XR engine
C366.definition: The XR engine, which is the middleware, utilizes the hardware resources to generate output.

C367.name: interactive systems
C367.definition: Interactive systems are a topic that includes their basic idea, how they differ from other systems, their design concerns, why they are important, and how XR relates to their development.

C368.name: Human factors
C368.definition: Human factors refers to the knowledge that helps a developer build better XR systems.

C369.name: Interaction design
C369.definition: Interaction design is important to give the user the ease of interacting with the system.

C370.name: Illusion of reality
C370.definition: The interaction and perceptual stimuli are supposed to be designed to create the best possible illusion of reality.

C371.name: Immersion
C371.definition: The feeling of perceiving that we are immersed.

C372.name: Perceptual system
C372.definition: The system that works by how our senses function and the physiology that drives our perception.

C373.name: Virtual world
C373.definition: The artificial world that our bodies are not designed to perceive.

C374.name: perceptual psychology
C374.definition: It is the science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena.

C375.name: Sensor
C375.definition: When referring to a device or system, a sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit.

C376.name: Human bodily sensors
C376.definition: In the context of the human body, these refer to an organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses.

C377.name: Photoreceptors
C377.definition: These are the receptors that are part of the vision sense, which uses electromagnetic energy as a stimulus.

C378.name: Mechanoreceptors
C378.definition: These are receptors used in various senses, including auditory, touch, balance, taste, and smell.

C379.name: Thermoreceptors
C379.definition: These are one of the two types of receptors involved in the touch sense.

C380.name: Chemoreceptors
C380.definition: These are receptors used in the sense of taste and smell, where chemical composition serves as the stimulus.

C381.name: Sensory system selectivity
C381.definition: This is the phenomenon where a receptor is designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

C382.name: Receptors
C382.definition: Receptors are bodily organs or sensors designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

C383.name: Perception
C383.definition: Perception is a higher level activity that occurs after sense organs convert stimuli into neural impulses.

C384.name: Cerebral cortex
C384.definition: The cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that handles perception and other functions like attention, memory, language, and consciousness.

C385.name: Dendrites
C385.definition: Dendrites are the input edges to a neuron node, allowing the neuron to aggregate information from other neurons.

C386.name: Axon
C386.definition: The axon is the output edge of a neuron, carrying impulses away from the cell body.

C387.name: Synapse
C387.definition: The synapse is the gap between the axon of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron through which electrical or chemical signals are passed.

C388.name: Sensory organs
C388.definition: These are the organs whose workings and implications for system design will be covered in detail in subsequent lectures.

C389.name: Hierarchical processing
C389.definition: This type of processing works in stages, allowing increasingly complex patterns to be detected in the stimulus.

C390.name: Selectivity
C390.definition: Selectivity is the idea that each receptor is susceptible to only one kind of stimulus.

C391.name: Lower-level information
C391.definition: This is the information derived directly from the initial inputs of receptors, such as R1 and R2.

C392.name: Stimuli interpretation
C392.definition: Stimuli interpretation is not based only on sensory inputs, but also depends on the kind of real-life experience knowledge a person possesses.

C393.name: Perceptual phenomena
C393.definition: Perceptual phenomena are the results of the combination of sensory input and knowledge, such as face recognition or identification of a song.

C394.name: Perceptual processing
C394.definition: Perceptual processing is the outcome of hierarchical processing combined with real-time sensory input and long-term knowledge or experience.

C395.name: Long-term memory
C395.definition: Long-term memory is knowledge or experience that has been gained or learned over a long period of time.

C396.name: sixth sense
C396.definition: It is a sense where we do not have a dedicated sensory organ or dedicated receptors to receive the stimuli, but we process information sent by the motor cortex.

C397.name: Brain development
C397.definition: It is basically learning the process of perception and learning the process of cognition over a long period of time.

C398.name: Human physiology
C398.definition: It is one of the basic components learned in the lecture, alongside psychology, in the context of designing VR systems.

C399.name: Natural lenses
C399.definition: Natural lenses are parts of the eyes.

C400.name: Combined system
C400.definition: The combined system of engineered and natural lenses helps us perceive the immersive visual content.

C401.name: Visual perception
C401.definition: Visual perception is the result when light is guided by lenses and arrives on the retina.

C402.name: Retina
C402.definition: This is the component at the back side of the eye where images are focused.

C403.name: photons
C403.definition: Photons are tiny particles of energy moving through space at high speeds.

C405.name: rays
C405.definition: A ray is a path which is assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon.

C406.name: transmission
C406.definition: Transmission is when light passes through the material and goes out of the material.

C407.name: absorption
C407.definition: Absorption is when the light rays terminate within the material or object.

C408.name: reflection
C408.definition: Reflection occurs when the ray falls on the surface and gets reflected from the surface without entering or penetrating the object.

C409.name: Ambient light
C409.definition: Ambient light is the light in the environment which gets reflected from the object surface along with light coming from the direct source.

C410.name: Perceived color
C410.definition: The perceived color is determined by the intensity of the light that reaches the viewer's eye.

C411.name: Intensity of light that reaches the viewer's eye
C411.definition: The intensity of the light that reaches the eye determines what color we are going to perceive.

C412.name: Human vision system
C412.definition: This is the system that the lecture will delve deeper into to gain a better understanding.

C413.name: Vision physiology
C413.definition: This is the specific aspect of vision that needs to be understood.

C414.name: Refraction
C414.definition: This is the process by which light rays are bent by the cornea and lens to focus images on the retina.

C415.name: Pupil
C415.definition: The pupil size can be changed (dilated or constricted) to let in more or less light.

C416.name: Iris
C416.definition: The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.

C417.name: Rods
C417.definition: Rods are photoreceptors that are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina.

C418.name: Cones
C418.definition: Cones are photoreceptors mainly located in a small central region of the retina called the fovea.

C419.name: Fovea
C419.definition: The central region of the retina that has the greatest concentration of cones.

C420.name: Photopic vision
C420.definition: Photopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with cones.

C421.name: Scotopic vision
C421.definition: Scotopic vision is the type of vision accomplished with rods only.

C422.name: Aqueous humor
C422.definition: Aqueous humor is a semi-liquid material found between the cornea and pupil.

C423.name: Vitreous humor
C423.definition: Vitreous humor is the material found between the lens and retina.

C424.name: Image acuity
C424.definition: Image acuity is a measure of image resolution, which is aided by having one optic nerve for each cone.

C425.name: visible light
C425.definition: Visible light refers to a spectrum or range of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves that we are able to perceive.

C426.name: perception of color
C426.definition: The perception of color is the process where light waves excite the cones in our eye.

C427.name: Central vision
C427.definition: Vision supported by the concentration of cones in the fovea, requiring the eyes to be pointed straight at a target to perceive a sharp color image.

C428.name: Peripheral vision
C428.definition: Vision supported by the peripheral region of the retina, which is better at detecting movement but cannot distinguish colors effectively.

C429.name: Peripheral region
C429.definition: The area of the retina where photoreceptor density is less, containing a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones.

C430.name: blind spot
C430.definition: The blind spot is a region in the eye where there are no photoreceptors, meaning we are blind to the light or visual stimuli that fall in that area.

C431.name: Human lens
C431.definition: It is a natural lens with variable focal depth.

C432.name: Image surface
C432.definition: It is the portion of the eye where the light rays fall, which is a non-planar surface.

C433.name: Engineered lens
C433.definition: An artificially created lens used in the setup.

C434.name: Focal depth
C434.definition: The distance between the lens and the focal point.

C435.name: Refractive index
C435.definition: The amount of light that passes through a medium.

C436.name: Focal plane
C436.definition: The plane where the converging parallel lights meet.

C437.name: Cornea
C437.definition: The cornea is considered one of the two effective convex lenses in the eye.

C438.name: Focal point
C438.definition: The focal point is the retina center onto which light is converged.

C439.name: Convergence
C439.definition: Convergence is the process required to cause parallel rays of light to be focused onto the retina center.

C440.name: Combined power
C440.definition: Combined power is the total optical power achieved when the diopters of the cornea and natural lens are added together.

C441.name: VR headset
C441.definition: A device constructed by placing a screen very close to the eyes, often utilizing a convex lens to fill the user's view.

C442.name: Convex lens
C442.definition: A lens used to increase optical power, functioning similarly to reading glasses, and helping focus the image onto the retina.

C443.name: Virtual image
C443.definition: The image that the screen appears to project, which is perceived as being enormous and infinitely far away.

C444.name: Artificial system
C444.definition: The setup comprising the screen and the engineered lens whose objective is to convert light into normal light that falls on the eye for perception.

C445.name: Binocular vision
C445.definition: This is the state where both eyes are used to see the same image within a common region.

C446.name: Translational
C446.definition: Translational movement is used for navigating in the 3D space.

C447.name: Rotational
C447.definition: Rotational movement is primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

C448.name: Degrees of freedom
C448.definition: Degrees of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space.

C449.name: Yaw
C449.definition: Yaw is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom.

C450.name: Roll
C450.definition: Roll is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom.

C451.name: Pitch
C451.definition: Pitch is one of the three rotational degrees of freedom.

C452.name: Photoreceptor density
C452.definition: A basic physiological property that directly impacts the engineering requirements for visual display hardware.

C453.name: Spatial resolution
C453.definition: The consideration of how many pixels per square area are needed.

C454.name: Intensity resolution and range
C454.definition: The measure of how many intensity values can be produced and what the minimum and maximum intensity values are.

C455.name: Temporal resolution
C455.definition: The consideration of how fast displays need to change their pixels.

C456.name: Frame rates
C456.definition: The rate at which displays refresh their pixels, which is particularly important in the context of motion perception.

C457.name: Aliasing
C457.definition: Aliasing is the appearance of jagged lines or staircases instead of smooth lines, especially when zooming out.

C458.name: Screen door effect
C458.definition: The screen door effect is an appearance where the image seems to have a screen on top of it, commonly seen in LCD projectors.

C459.name: Retina display
C459.definition: A retina display is a type of display where the supported resolution is a minimum of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi).

C460.name: Auditory senses
C460.definition: The topic of the lecture, which involves discussing the auditory sense and physiology of hearing and its relevance for extended reality experiences.

C461.name: Human factors
C461.definition: The ideas that influence the design and overall experience of interactive systems.

C462.name: Extended reality systems
C462.definition: The systems for which human factors are relevant and which are the focus of the detailed discussion.

C463.name: Audio recording and reproduction
C463.definition: The process of recording sound (speech or non-speech) and reproducing it, which can be considered a VR experience in itself.

C464.name: Believable experience
C464.definition: An experience that is reinforced by audio, making it closer to reality and closer to everyday experiences.

C465.name: Emotional connection
C465.definition: An attachment to the environment that can be increased when vision is coupled with audio.

C466.name: Sound
C466.definition: Sound is nothing but vibration in a medium, which can be air, water, or other gases, liquids, and solids.

C467.name: Sound wave
C467.definition: A sound wave is a plot of pressure variation against time.

C468.name: Frequency
C468.definition: Frequency is the number of alterations between one maximum to another maximum per second, measured in Hertz.

C469.name: Amplitude
C469.definition: Amplitude is defined as the maximum displacement from the mean or rest position of the wave.

C470.name: Phase
C470.definition: Phase is the start position of a cycle of the wave, which can begin at 0 to 360 degrees.

C471.name: Decompression extreme
C471.definition: Decompression extreme, also called rarefaction extreme, means the pressure is very low.

C472.name: canal
C472.definition: The canal works as an amplifier, boosting the sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

C473.name: tympanic membrane
C473.definition: The tympanic membrane is the membrane that vibrates when struck by the wave.

C474.name: ossicles
C474.definition: The ossicles are three bones (malleus, incus, and stapes) that transfer vibration from the middle ear.

C475.name: cochlea
C475.definition: The cochlea is the sense organ for hearing that converts sound energy to neural impulses.

C476.name: outer ear
C476.definition: The outer ear is the initial part of the hearing system that receives the sound wave.

C477.name: inner ear
C477.definition: The inner ear is the final part of the hearing system that houses the cochlea.

C478.name: Neural impulses
C478.definition: Neural impulses are the signals that sound waves are converted into through the mechanisms of the ear.

C479.name: Middle ear
C479.definition: The middle ear is one of the three parts of the ear.

C480.name: Sound perception
C480.definition: This is the process by which we perceive sound, which occurs at three levels.

C481.name: Social level
C481.definition: This perception helps us carry out social interactions with other individuals.

C482.name: Psychophysics
C482.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that are produced by physical stimuli.

C483.name: Psychoacoustics
C483.definition: Psychoacoustics is a more specific area of psychophysics where the term physical is replaced with the term acoustic, studying phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli or sound.

C484.name: Weber's law
C484.definition: Weber's law is a law that captures Just noticeable difference, represented as delta M by M equals C.

C485.name: Stevens' Power Law
C485.definition: This law describes how perception changes moderately even when the physical stimuli changes to a much higher degree, following the formula P = C * m to the power x.

C486.name: Just Noticeable Difference
C486.definition: This is the threshold change required for a change to be perceived, or the range below which a change is not perceived.

C487.name: Auditory Perception
C487.definition: This refers to our perception when physical stimuli are replaced with acoustic stimuli.

C488.name: Pitch perception
C488.definition: Pitch perception is the ability to perceive the frequency of a sound wave.

C489.name: Localization
C489.definition: Localization deals with estimating the location of a sound source by hearing it.

C490.name: Azimuth
C490.definition: This is the angle in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the source of the sound.

C491.name: Elevation
C491.definition: This is the angle between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane.

C492.name: Radius
C492.definition: The source is called the radius, which is the distance from the origin (the human head) to the source.

C493.name: Head-related transfer functions
C493.definition: HRTF models how we receive sound from a location in space.

C494.name: Non-stationary
C494.definition: Non-stationary means that the auditory component is moving with the user.

C495.name: Interactive
C495.definition: Interactive means that the auditory component is dependent on the listener's actions.

C496.name: Binaural sound
C496.definition: Binaural sound is synthesized using a pair of HRTF for both ears.

C497.name: Proprioceptive sense or proprioception
C497.definition: This is introduced as the sixth sense, alongside the five traditional senses.

C498.name: Full immersive experience
C498.definition: This is the context for the discussion regarding the role of senses other than visual and auditory.

C499.name: Human visual perceptual system
C499.definition: This system's knowledge helps in building better XR systems.

C500.name: Human auditory system
C500.definition: This system helps create immersive experience in XR in addition to the visual perceptual system.

C501.name: Touch sense
C501.definition: The touch sense is a human sense related to the perception of touch and is supported by dedicated receptors.

C502.name: Proprioception
C502.definition: Proprioception is the awareness of the pose of each movable human body part, which is sometimes referred to as our sixth sense.

C503.name: Kinesthesis
C503.definition: Kinesthesis provides information on velocities, acceleration, and forces while moving the body parts.

C504.name: Somatosensory system
C504.definition: The somatosensory system is a sensory organ that handles touch, proprioception, and kinesthesis.

C505.name: Haptic perception
C505.definition: Haptic perception is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects.

C506.name: Haptic exploration
C506.definition: Haptic exploration involves object handling or manipulation to infer the overall geometric shape of an object.

C507.name: Muscle spindles
C507.definition: Muscle spindles are receptors embedded inside each muscle that report to the brain on changes in length.

C508.name: Force feedback
C508.definition: A method of providing touch sensation stimuli as output, typically in the form of vibrations, which is common in many XR systems.

C509.name: Haptic pin array
C509.definition: A matrix of pins controlled by a computer that is forced upward to simulate various textures as a fingertip scans across its surface.

C510.name: Tangible user interfaces
C510.definition: Real-world objects that are used to provide touch sensation feedback, replacing computer-controlled haptic devices.

C511.name: Chemical senses
C511.definition: These senses are generally grouped together because the receptors work by chemical interaction with the molecules that arrive on them.

C512.name: Taste/Smell
C512.definition: Taste or smell is nothing but a chemical reaction of the chemoreceptors with the stimuli that are arriving to the receptors.

C513.name: Smell interfaces
C513.definition: These are devices meant for providing stimuli to our nose, usually involving air pumps that spray chemical compounds into the air.

C514.name: Olfactory displays
C514.definition: This is a term used to call smell interfaces, which are generic displays designed to provide olfactory stimuli.

C515.name: Taste interfaces
C515.definition: These are systems, such as those using electrodes placed over and under the tongue, designed to simulate the main taste types.

C516.name: Immersion
C516.definition: Immersion is a state that can be increased in a VR or XR setting when appropriate support is provided.

C517.name: XR systems
C517.definition: XR systems are a class of interactive systems because the users of these systems are supposed to be laypersons.

C518.name: Interactive system
C518.definition: An interactive system is application software designed for laypersons who do not need to know how the hardware or software works.

C519.name: Extended Reality Systems
C519.definition: These are the specific type of interactive systems that the course is focusing on.

C520.name: Usability
C520.definition: Usability refers to a system being evaluated based on a specific group of users, a specified context of use, and specific tasks.

C521.name: User-centric software
C521.definition: User-centric software is designed to be usable systems that cater to the needs and expectations of laypersons.

C522.name: Software development life cycle
C522.definition: It is followed to develop and deploy software so as to comprehensively capture and represent the design and development activities that should go into building the software.

C523.name: Software engineering
C523.definition: It is a single term used to represent the idea of software development life cycle, or engineering a software.

C524.name: Stages
C524.definition: They capture or structure the whole process and through their connection, they essentially let us represent in a very structured manner how the development process should take place.

C525.name: design space
C525.definition: The set of all possible designs.

C526.name: Highly iterative lifecycle
C526.definition: A highly iterative lifecycle is required to implement a user-centric design approach for building interactive software, allowing for frequent looping to account for user feedback.

C527.name: Design prototype evaluate cycle
C527.definition: This cycle comprises the design stage, prototyping stage, and early evaluation stage.

C528.name: Code testing
C528.definition: Testing that ensures there are no bugs and the code executes properly.

C529.name: Requirement gathering stage
C529.definition: This is a common stage where we check for the feasibility of the project in terms of available resources, money, and time, and involve end users along with the client.

C530.name: Interface design
C530.definition: This is one of the two parts of designing the system within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, focusing on the user's point of view.

C531.name: Code design
