C531.definition: This is a design part that is separate from the design-prototype-evaluate cycle and deals with coding.

C532.name: Requirement analysis
C532.definition: When referring to requirement analysis, it typically refers to the requirements of the client.

C533.name: Early evaluation
C533.definition: Evaluating the ideas of interface and interaction design quickly with fewer resources and less time.

C534.name: Empirical study
C534.definition: A stage required to ensure the product conforms to usability, which involves systematic testing with the end users.

C535.name: Interactive System Development Lifecycle
C535.definition: It is the overall idea of what should be done to build interactive systems which are usable.

C536.name: Usable System
C536.definition: It is the desired outcome of the overall process of building interactive systems.

C537.name: Case study
C537.definition: A practical system used to understand different aspects of system development.

C538.name: Digital preservation of physical heritage
C538.definition: The process of preserving the heritage of the Majuli River Island in the digital space.

C539.name: Virtual reality system
C539.definition: A system used to digitally preserve the Majuli River Islands' ecological and cultural heritage.

C540.name: Tangible heritage
C540.definition: Tangible heritage aspects refer to heritage aspects of the island which someone can touch and feel, such as cultural artifacts or architectural aspects.

C541.name: Intangible heritage
C541.definition: Intangible heritage aspects cannot be touched and felt, but they can be sensed through different means, including traditional skills and knowledge.

C542.name: Cultural heritage
C542.definition: Cultural heritage consists of two broad aspects: tangible heritage and intangible heritage.

C543.name: Integration of man and nature
C543.definition: The island's unique position led to a distinctive integration of man and nature.

C544.name: ecological heritage
C544.definition: This refers to the flora and fauna of the island which exist due to its unique geology, geography, and topography.

C545.name: digital preservation
C545.definition: This is the necessary action taken because the island is constantly being hit by severe annual floods and erosion, which threatens its existence.

C546.name: erosion
C546.definition: Erosion is the process where the island is slowly consumed by the river and reduced in size due to severe annual floods.

C547.name: Digital heritage preservation
C547.definition: It is the process of using digital media to preserve heritage, which can be cultural, educational, scientific, or ecological.

C548.name: Archiving
C548.definition: Archiving means storing the visual and audio files that capture the information heritage of a particular entity, object, space, or place.

C549.name: Heritage preservation
C549.definition: Heritage preservation involves creating an archive of heritage information which ideally should be in the form of multimedia comprising images, videos, audios, and texts.

C550.name: Experiencing the heritage
C550.definition: Experiencing the heritage refers to a virtual tour or an exploration of the island utilizing the archival information.

C551.name: Archive of heritage information
C551.definition: The archive of heritage information is created during heritage preservation and comprises multimedia such as images, videos, audios, and texts.

C552.name: Use case
C552.definition: A use case describes what a system is all about and why it needs to be built.

C553.name: Immersive virtual tours
C553.definition: These are experiences through which the heritage is experienced, forming one component of the digital heritage preservation system.

C554.name: Satras
C554.definition: These are Vaishnavite monasteries that serve as centers of religious significance and cultural vitality on the island.

C555.name: Hot spots
C555.definition: These are specific points created on a map of the island where the tangible and intangible aspects of the cultural landscape are captured.

C556.name: Multimodal archive
C556.definition: This is the archive created to preserve the heritage aspects of the island, utilizing various data types like images, videos, and textual descriptions.

C557.name: Usability testing
C557.definition: Testing that focuses on how well a system works for the user, rather than only testing the code.

C558.name: Tangible and intangible heritage
C558.definition: The vast information, both physical and non-physical, that is being preserved and explored in the virtual tour.

C559.name: System-Centered Design
C559.definition: A design approach where the development is driven by the skill and interest of the developer or manager rather than the needs and expectations of the user.

C560.name: Requirement Gathering
C560.definition: The process of learning about the methods for gathering end user requirements so that usability is ensured.

C561.name: Specification
C561.definition: Something that is required for system implementation.

C562.name: Usability requirements
C562.definition: Requirements that relate to ensuring the system is usable.

C563.name: End user requirements
C563.definition: Requirements specific to the end user, as opposed to client requirements.

C564.name: Requirement
C564.definition: In this context, the term requirement specifically refers to end user requirements.

C565.name: Feasibility
C565.definition: These are requirements related to the first stage, such as deciding on mobile platforms or programming languages.

C566.name: Code design stage
C566.definition: This stage involves questions about how to store various information, such as whether to use RDBMS tools like MySQL.

C567.name: System specification
C567.definition: This is the outcome that requirements lead to.

C568.name: usability
C568.definition: Usability is the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use.

C569.name: Functional requirements
C569.definition: These are system features and abilities of the system to carry out tasks in terms of some functions which are treated as black boxes.

C570.name: Quality attributes
C570.definition: These are characteristics that usability requirements are typically related to.

C571.name: interface issues
C571.definition: Interface issues refer to the design or qualities of the interface that should be usable, making the interface usable.

C572.name: external system interface
C572.definition: The external system interface involves hardware and software interfacing, as well as the interfacing between the hardware and software.

C573.name: user interface
C573.definition: The user interface is the area where usability issues come into the picture.

C574.name: requirement gathering methods
C574.definition: Requirement gathering methods are the techniques that can be deployed to gather requirements and ensure usability.

C575.name: Contextual inquiry
C575.definition: A requirement gathering method that gathers end user requirements by observing users in their natural work setting.

C576.name: Natural work setting
C576.definition: The specified context where users are observed performing tasks to gather requirements.

C577.name: Semi-structured interview process
C577.definition: A method of contextual inquiry that consists of both interviews and observations.

C578.name: Usability requirement gathering
C578.definition: An essential part of ensuring a usable design, which allows for a proper design that takes care of users' needs and expectations.

C579.name: Contextual inquiry
C579.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method used to observe targeted groups of users in their natural work setting to understand how they behave and what they do.

C580.name: Passive mode
C580.definition: In passive mode, user activities are recorded or videotaped, and the activities are then observed later by the observer.

C581.name: Master apprentice model
C581.definition: The master apprentice model requires the observer to act as an apprentice and treat the users as masters during the inquiry.

C583.name: Execute stage
C583.definition: This is the stage where the actual inquiry takes place.

C584.name: Initiate stage
C584.definition: This stage requires contacting authorities for necessary permissions and opening communication with end users.

C585.name: Execute test stage
C585.definition: This stage is where the actual observation is performed and data is recorded.

C586.name: Close stage
C586.definition: This stage involves formally closing the activity, ideally by sending thank you notes to the users.

C587.name: Reflect stage
C587.definition: In this stage, the observer or experimental team analyzes the collected data and identifies the design goals.

C588.name: Design goals
C588.definition: These are the objectives that are identified by analyzing the data collected during the execute stage.

C589.name: Affinity diagram method
C589.definition: This is a technique used to arrange data to easily find patterns, which then leads to the design specification of the design goals.

C590.name: Data
C590.definition: The data is essentially the notes taken by the observers while observing the behavior.

C591.name: Idea
C591.definition: An idea is called a note when following the affinity diagram.

C592.name: Physical note-taking
C592.definition: This is the traditional method of taking notes, typically done on pen and paper.

C593.name: Generate and display the ideas
C593.definition: This refers to the combined process of generating ideas and then showing those ideas, as part of the affinity diagram method.

C594.name: Groups
C594.definition: Groups are formed by identifying patterns among ideas so that similar ideas with similar patterns can be sorted into a single group.

C595.name: Sorting of the ideas into groups
C595.definition: This is the stage where ideas are sorted into groups by identifying patterns among them so that similar ideas can be grouped together.

C596.name: Content management
C596.definition: Content management is a common idea that relates issues such as content relocation not being possible and erasing content being a daunting task.

C597.name: Header
C597.definition: A header is a name provided for the pattern which binds multiple ideas together.

C598.name: Idea generation
C598.definition: Idea generation refers to the final note that is taken by the observer.

C599.name: Display
C599.definition: The display is the place where the notes are put together, which can be a wall or a board.

C600.name: Final drawing
C600.definition: The final drawing is essentially sorting all the ideas into groups.

C601.name: Design Recommendation
C601.definition: Design recommendations are a set of suggestions that can be developed based on the collected data.

C602.name: Informed design choice
C602.definition: An informed design choice is one where the information used comes through methods like contextual inquiry, ensuring user needs and expectations are met.

C603.name: Prescription for implementation
C603.definition: A prescription for implementation is not the requirement, as it specifies how to implement the requirement.

C604.name: Contextual inquiry
C604.definition: This is a usability requirement gathering method that the discussion has started.

C605.name: Requirement gathering
C605.definition: This is the process of gathering usability requirements for the users and the tour.

C606.name: Guidelines
C606.definition: Guidelines are framed based on observations to suggest what the app should do or should not do.

C607.name: Software requirements specification
C607.definition: The Software Requirements Specification (SRS) is a document used for specifying all types of requirements, including both functional and non-functional.

C608.name: Functional requirement specification
C608.definition: This is the formal representation or specification of requirements within the SRS document.

C609.name: Know the user
C609.definition: This is the first stage of the process, which involves understanding the target audience.

C610.name: Functional specifications
C610.definition: Functional specifications are one possible outcome of utilizing the result of the analysis, alongside guidelines.

C611.name: Data subset
C611.definition: A limited portion of the total data that is made accessible to each specific group of users.

C612.name: Design challenges
C612.definition: Key problems that must be addressed during the development process.

C613.name: Location awareness
C613.definition: It is the crucial process of ensuring users have accurate location information to prevent disorientation, especially when dealing with large geographies.

C614.name: Tangible and intangible heritage experience
C614.definition: This refers to the required provision of both tangible and intangible heritage experiences to the user.

C615.name: Interaction aid for enhanced user experience
C615.definition: This challenge involves providing support that includes navigation support, user-friendly interfaces, and increasing presence through natural interactions.

C616.name: Design language
C616.definition: A design language is needed to express the design, allowing for brainstorming or refinement.

C617.name: Interface and interaction design
C617.definition: This is the subject matter being discussed, focusing on how to start and represent a design.

C618.name: Creative thinking process
C618.definition: This is a process where design can start by relying on creativity, which may be aided by intuition, experience, or domain knowledge.

C619.name: Heuristics
C619.definition: Heuristics are guidelines, along with checklists and thumb rules, that can act as a starting point to aid creative thinking.

C620.name: Prototype
C620.definition: A prototype can be thought of as a language to express design ideas and can be considered a language for interface design.

C621.name: Generic guidelines
C621.definition: These guidelines are very broad in nature, small in size, and cover broad aspects of interactive systems at a high level.

C622.name: Specification of design
C622.definition: This essentially refers to the language used to express whatever we are thinking about the design.

C623.name: Specific guideline set
C623.definition: Guidelines that are typically applicable to a specific domain, such as VR or immersive systems, often related to minimizing cyber sickness.

C624.name: Consistency
C624.definition: The principle that an interface design must maintain uniformity in its elements and interactions throughout the system.

C625.name: Internal consistency
C625.definition: The practice of utilizing the same elements and interactions for the same tasks across different parts of the design.

C626.name: External consistency
C626.definition: The principle that the system's elements and interactions should closely match the user's real-world knowledge and experience.

C627.name: Hotkeys
C627.definition: Hotkeys are a combination of keys used to perform an action, such as saving a document.

C628.name: Universal usability
C628.definition: Universal usability is the design principle that requires facilities for all classes of users.

C629.name: Informative feedback
C629.definition: Feedback that is given to the user after an action to inform them about the system's status or progress.

C630.name: Progress bar
C630.definition: A visual element that appears to show the percentage of tasks completed during an operation.

C631.name: Usable design
C631.definition: A design quality where the user can understand what the system is doing, whether a task is getting done, and how much of the task is completed.

C632.name: Storage metaphor
C632.definition: A representation, such as a floppy disk icon, used to represent the concept of storage.

C633.name: Design dialogues to yield closure
C633.definition: Designing the system so that the user feels the task is started, executed, and finally completed.

C634.name: Beginning part, middle part, and an end part
C634.definition: The required organizational structure for task execution, ensuring the user understands the flow of the process.

C635.name: Error prevention and simple error handling
C635.definition: This design principle involves trying to minimize user errors and providing simple information if an error does occur.

C636.name: Reversal of action
C636.definition: This is a design objective that allows users to return from an erroneous situation after making a mistake.

C637.name: Keeping the users in control
C637.definition: This means letting users feel that they are in control of the system, which is important for usability.

C638.name: Perceive their interaction
C638.definition: Users should be able to understand and perceive that something is happening, which signifies a change in system state.

C639.name: Feedback
C639.definition: The result of user actions should be made aware of, meaning the user should be able to see the outcome of their actions.

C640.name: Short term memory
C640.definition: It is a kind of notes or non-permanent storage used to aid day-to-day activities.

C641.name: Long term memory
C641.definition: This is permanent storage from which information is brought into short-term memory to aid activities.

C642.name: 7 plus or minus 2 rule
C642.definition: This rule states that it is best to keep between 5 to 9 chunks of information in short-term memory at one time.

C643.name: Chunk of information
C643.definition: This refers to a unit of information that should ideally be kept between 5 to 9 for optimum user outcome.

C644.name: Reduce short term memory load
C644.definition: This is a rule suggesting that the design should not force users to remember too many things.

C645.name: Object interaction
C645.definition: The selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment.

C646.name: Navigation
C646.definition: The act of moving from one point to another within the virtual environment.

C647.name: Interaction for system control
C647.definition: System-related settings interaction required to change those settings.

C648.name: Interaction for selection
C648.definition: This type of interaction involves selecting the object with which the user wants to interact.

C649.name: Interaction for manipulation
C649.definition: This interaction occurs after selection and changes the properties of the object.

C650.name: Object selection
C650.definition: This refers to specifying one or more objects from a set of virtual objects that are part of the virtual world.

C651.name: Target occlusion
C651.definition: This is a challenging task where a target object is partly or fully hidden by other surrounding objects.

C652.name: Hand selection
C652.definition: This is a method where the user uses their hand to select objects in a virtual world.

C653.name: Pointing-based selection
C653.definition: This is a method used to select objects in a virtual world.

C654.name: Image plane selection
C654.definition: This technique involves the user holding one or two hands between the eye and the desired object, and then providing a signal to select the object when it lines up with the hand and eye.

C655.name: Hand selection technique
C655.definition: This technique involves selecting virtual objects in the virtual world using the hand.

C656.name: Virtual hand
C656.definition: It is an avatar of the physical hand that is visible in the virtual world.

C657.name: Go-go technique
C657.definition: This technique allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length to select distant objects without tiring.

C658.name: Prism
C658.definition: This is an improvement of the go-go technique that applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's hand is moving below a specified speed.

C659.name: Intent-driven selection
C659.definition: This technique uses gestures or the posture of the virtual fingers as an indication of the user's level of confidence in selecting an object.

C660.name: Proximity spheres
C660.definition: These spheres are used to progressively refine the selection of an object based on hand postures.

C661.name: Ray casting
C661.definition: A basic technique where the user points at objects with a virtual ray.

C662.name: Bend cast
C662.definition: A technique where the system bends the ray towards the object closest to the path.

C663.name: Depth ray
C663.definition: An improvement over the basic ray casting method used to disambiguate between objects when the pointing vector hits multiple targets.

C664.name: Hand pointing
C664.definition: Pointing done using the hand or handheld input devices.

C665.name: Eye gaze pointing
C665.definition: Extending the ray using eye gaze controlling devices or eye trackers, changing pointing with eye gaze.

C666.name: Volumetric selection
C666.definition: This technique enables the user to select a 3D region in space, which then selects corresponding objects within that space.

C667.name: Head crusher technique
C667.definition: The user positions the thumb and the forefinger around the desired object such that the object is enclosed by the thumb and forefinger in the 2D image plane.

C668.name: Cone casting flashlight technique
C668.definition: A cone is cast to a distance, and objects within the cone get selected, extending the ray casting idea.

C669.name: Sphere casting flashlight technique
C669.definition: A sphere is cast onto the nearest intersected surface, and the objects found within the sphere are selected.

C670.name: Two-handed box selection technique
C670.definition: The user uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box or a cube to select a specified region of the 3D space.

C671.name: Manipulation
C671.definition: Manipulation is the process of modifying an object's properties, such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.

C672.name: Hand manipulation
C672.definition: Hand manipulation uses a virtual hand, smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controller-based interaction to manipulate objects.

C673.name: Indirect manipulation
C673.definition: Indirect manipulation involves manipulating other objects that are mapped to the desired virtual object, thereby manipulating the desired object without direct interaction.

C674.name: World in miniature
C674.definition: World in miniature (WIM) provides the user a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, allowing indirect manipulation of virtual objects.

C675.name: Locomotion
C675.definition: Locomotion is the travel part of navigation, which is the motor component of navigation.

C676.name: Exploration
C676.definition: Exploration is a type of travel where there is no explicit goal to reach, and the user simply wants to move around to see or learn things.

C677.name: Search
C677.definition: Search involves searching for or moving to a specified target location.

C678.name: Locomotion techniques
C678.definition: These are the four broad types of techniques used to accomplish travel from one point to another.

C679.name: Walking-based locomotion
C679.definition: Traveling in the virtual world by physically walking in the physical world or the real world.

C680.name: Partial gait technique
C680.definition: A technique where the user walks but remains in the same physical place, and the walking pattern is mapped to different types of walking in the virtual space.

C681.name: Gait negation technique
C681.definition: A technique where specialized setup cancels the user's lateral movements while keeping their physical position fixed, allowing movement to be mapped to a specific virtual movement.

C682.name: steering-based navigation
C682.definition: This category indicates continuous control of direction and speed while the user is moving from one point to another.

C683.name: spatial steering-based navigation
C683.definition: In this case, the navigation is controlled using the user's body parts.

C684.name: physical steering-based locomotion technique
C684.definition: This technique involves some physical setups and separate hardware, such as bike locomotion platforms or VR simulators.

C685.name: selection-based navigation
C685.definition: This technique allows users to focus on where to go rather than how to get there.

C686.name: target selection-based locomotion
C686.definition: In this technique, the user selects the destination or target where they want to move, and the virtual viewpoint changes.

C687.name: manipulation-based locomotion techniques
C687.definition: Locomotion works by manipulating the user's position, orientation, or scale using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

C688.name: Wayfinding
C688.definition: Wayfinding refers to location awareness and ascertaining a path through the environment to the desired destination.

C689.name: Cognitive map
C689.definition: A cognitive map is a mental model or map of the surroundings and overall environment.

C690.name: Mental model
C690.definition: A mental model is essentially a cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment.

C691.name: Landmark knowledge
C691.definition: Landmark knowledge is knowledge about landmarks in surroundings or other places.

C692.name: Procedural knowledge
C692.definition: Procedural knowledge is the sequence of actions required to follow a path.

C693.name: Topological knowledge
C693.definition: Topological knowledge is the overall map-like knowledge of the environment.

C694.name: Wayfinding support
C694.definition: Wayfinding support is required for a system to provide a good immersive user experience, ensuring travel supports are effectively used while performing navigation.

C695.name: Landmark
C695.definition: A landmark is any obvious distinct non-mobile object that is positioned in a given place and can be seen from several locations.

C696.name: Path following
C696.definition: Path following is a wayfinding support where multiple paths through a single space may be denoted by colors so that the user knows there are different paths to reach a destination.

C697.name: Breadcrumbs
C697.definition: Breadcrumbs is a support that involves leaving a trail of the path followed by predecessors, allowing users to know when they have been somewhere before.

C698.name: multimodal interaction techniques for system control
C698.definition: These techniques involve combining multiple interaction methods, such as combining voice with gestures.

C699.name: navigation interaction
C699.definition: Navigation interaction comprises the processes of travel and wayfinding.

C700.name: Enhance the user's presence
C700.definition: This objective is to ensure that the users feel immersed and present within the virtual environment.

C701.name: Minimize cyber sickness
C701.definition: This objective was to design the tour to be comfortable and to minimize any risk of cyber sickness.

C702.name: Interactive system development lifecycle model
C702.definition: This model involves continuously refining design ideas based on feedback and observations by involving the end users.

C703.name: Distinct categories
C703.definition: These are groups of users that each possess their own unique preferences for visiting or exploring the island.

C704.name: Contextual inquiry methods
C704.definition: These methods are used to collect specific preferences from users to tailor the content and features of the virtual tour.

C705.name: Points of interest
C705.definition: These are the specific locations on the island, such as satras, villages, and towns, that are marked and need to be covered by the tour.

C706.name: curved screen
C706.definition: A design element that shows content in an immersive setting.

C707.name: immersive setting
C707.definition: A setting where the screen is curved and shows content to the user.

C708.name: boat ride experience
C708.definition: An element added to give the user the feeling of being transported from one bank of the river to the other.

C709.name: 360-degree boat ride video
C709.definition: The method used to give the user the feeling of actually traveling through a boat.

C710.name: user group
C710.definition: A category of users, such as pilgrims, students, or tourists, that the user can choose before the experience begins.

C711.name: Pre-processing
C711.definition: Pre-processing is the initial processing of collected content, such as images and videos, to improve the visual appearance and user experience.

C712.name: Uniform illumination
C712.definition: Uniform illumination is the process of editing images and videos to ensure that the same illumination effect is present across all images, regardless of when they were taken.

C713.name: 360-degree images
C713.definition: 360-degree images are images used to create scenes where the user is traveling from one image to another.

C714.name: Virtual tablet
C714.definition: The virtual tablet acts as the main interface, providing navigation tools, a video player, and access to information content.

C715.name: Interactive tablet interface
C715.definition: This is a provided interface that users utilize for interaction and navigation.

C716.name: Video player
C716.definition: A component integrated into the tablet interface that allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to their current location in the virtual world.

C717.name: Minimap concept
C717.definition: The minimap concept is useful to provide a sense of belonging or sense of orientation to a place.

C718.name: World-in-miniature type of map
C718.definition: This type of map provides a miniature representation of the entire island or a specific place on the island.

C719.name: Dual maps
C719.definition: Dual maps consist of a global map and a local map, which are used to reduce clutter and provide clear navigation support.

C720.name: Dynamic orientation awareness
C720.definition: This feature provides users with spatial orientation, helping them know in which direction to move.

C721.name: Tablet interface
C721.definition: The interface that includes the video player and allows users to access cultural and ecological videos relevant to the current user location.

C722.name: View interpolation technique
C722.definition: A technique that blurs the boundaries between two images to ensure a smooth feeling of transitioning from one image to another.

C723.name: Virtual vehicle metaphor
C723.definition: A 3D model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within the tour.

C724.name: Selection-based locomotion technique
C724.definition: A technique where the user selects a destination using pre-planned routes, rather than instantaneous movement.

C725.name: Ray casting interactions
C725.definition: An interaction method that allows the user to operate the vehicle and provide direction of movement.

C726.name: Informative notifications and descriptions
C726.definition: Elements that provide additional context about locations and significant spots, enriching the user's understanding and engagement.

C727.name: Directional arrows
C727.definition: Elements added to make the user aware of points of interest by guiding them on which way to move.

C728.name: Information icons
C728.definition: Icons that provide further details about a place upon interaction, usually in the form of textual information.

C729.name: Controlled navigation technique
C729.definition: A technique where users can navigate or teleport using a joystick, which reduces abrupt movements that can cause discomfort.

C730.name: Design
C730.definition: In this context, design refers to interface and interaction design, not the code design.

C731.name: Consistent visual cues
C731.definition: These cues are implemented in the design to help maintain spatial orientation and reduce sensory conflicts.

C732.name: Smooth transitions
C732.definition: These transitions are implemented in the design to help maintain spatial orientation and reduce sensory conflicts.
